title: DNS Security
summary: DNS security covers the protection of the domain name system itself and the defensive use of DNS data. The domain name system is a globally distributed, largely unauthenticated directory that turns names into addresses, so it is both an attractive target and a rich source of evidence. Attacks against it include cache poisoning, where forged answers are planted in a resolver so many users are misdirected; tunnelling, where data is smuggled inside query names to bypass egress controls; abuse of open resolvers to reflect and amplify traffic at a victim; and hijacking of registrar or DNS provider accounts to redirect a whole domain. Defensive practice therefore has two sides. On the infrastructure side it means redundant and locked-down resolvers, registrar protections that require strong authentication and transfer locks, careful record hygiene, and response validation. On the detection side it means logging queries and watching for unusual volumes, strange record types, long or high-entropy names, and lookups to newly registered or reputation-poor domains. The mistake people usually make is treating DNS as plumbing nobody would attack, which is exactly why so much malicious traffic hides there.

beginner.definition: DNS security means protecting the service that turns website names into addresses, and using its records to spot attacks. That service is called the domain name system. When it is tricked or badly configured, users can be sent to the wrong place without noticing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Almost every connection starts with a name lookup, so attackers aim at it first. A poisoned answer can send your staff to a fake login page. Hidden data can slip out through lookups that look normal. Because the traffic is so common, bad activity blends in easily. Strong DNS protection and good logging close a gap that most tools ignore.
howItWorks: Names are resolved through a chain of servers, and an answer can be altered at several points.
If a resolver accepts a forged answer, it stores it and misdirects many later users.
Attackers can encode stolen data inside long query names to slip past a firewall.
Your own domain can be redirected if a registrar or provider account is taken over.
Defenders lock down accounts, run trusted resolvers and keep records accurate.
Teams log queries and alert on odd volumes, odd record types and unknown domains.
beginner.example: Think of a post office that forwards letters by name. A dishonest clerk can swap an address label, so your letter goes to a thief instead of the bank. Or someone can smuggle a note out by writing it in tiny letters on the front of an envelope. Both abuses look like ordinary post, which is why the postmaster must check and record the traffic.
takeaways: Protect the resolvers and the accounts that control your domain names.
Log queries, because DNS records reveal attacks that other logs miss.
Treat strange lookup patterns, such as very long names, as a warning sign.

objectives: Explain what the domain name system does and why it is a target worth defending.
Describe how cache poisoning misdirects many users through a single wrong answer.
Recognise how hidden data transfer can be carried inside DNS queries.
List practical protections for resolvers, domain records and registrar accounts.
Identify DNS log signals that help detect malicious or unusual activity.
